What the official sources say

  • Adverse possession rebuts the presumption of owner possession if property was held and possessed adversely to legal title for at least seven years before the action. (Utah Code 78B-2-208(2); source)
  • Adverse possession may not be established unless the land was occupied and claimed continuously for seven years and the party and predecessors/grantors paid all taxes levied and assessed on the land (property tax payment is required). (Utah Code 78B-2-214; source)
  • Under a written document purporting to convey title (or a court decree/judgment conveying title), property is adversely held if the possessor has occupied it continuously for at least seven years; possession of one lot in a divided tract is not possession of another lot. (Utah Code 78B-2-210; source)
  • An owner or authorized agent may ask law enforcement to immediately remove a trespasser by attesting: unlawful entry, property not open to the public, owner directed the trespasser to leave, not a current/former tenant under a written rental agreement, not an immediate family member, and no pending litigation between them. (Utah Code 78B-6-817(1) (eff. 5/7/2025); source)
  • The owner submits a verified, penalty-of-perjury Complaint to Remove Trespassers with proof of ownership; law enforcement serves a notice to immediately vacate (hand delivery or posting), puts the owner in possession, and may arrest for trespass or other cause. (Utah Code 78B-6-817(2)-(3); source)

Utah Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Utah house?

Check the statute and talk to a Utah attorney about your facts.

Can a squatter become the owner of a Utah house?

Only through adverse possession, and Utah makes that hard. The law starts from the presumption that the person holding legal title is the one in possession, and anyone else's occupation is treated as subordinate to that title.

Utah Code 78B-2-208 allows that presumption to be rebutted only by showing the property was held and possessed adversely to the legal title for at least seven years before the action began. A short stay in a vacant house, however unwelcome, does not come close.

What must a Utah adverse possession claim prove?

The claimant must show continuous occupation and a claim of right for seven years, and that taxes on the land were paid. Utah Code 78B-2-214 bars a claim unless the party and the party's predecessors and grantors paid all taxes levied and assessed on the land.

That tax requirement does a lot of work. A person who sneaks into a house and never pays the county cannot meet it. Utah also separates two kinds of claim.

  • Claim under a written instrument or court judgment: seven years of continuous occupation while holding a document that purports to convey title (78B-2-210).
  • Claim with no document: only the land actually occupied counts, and the occupation must be continued, under a claim of title and exclusive of any other right (78B-2-212).

What counts as possession under a written instrument?

Land is treated as possessed if it has been usually cultivated or improved, protected by a substantial enclosure, or used for fuel, fencing timber, husbandry, pasturage or the ordinary use of the occupant. Those tests come from Utah Code 78B-2-211.

The statute also covers a known farm or single lot that is partly improved: the uncleared part is treated as occupied for the same time as the improved part. For lots in a divided tract, possession of one lot is not possession of another lot in the same tract. That limit matters for subdivisions, where a neighbor's use of an extra parcel does not stretch to cover the whole tract.

What do the Utah adverse possession rules look like side by side?

The table summarizes the provisions most owners ask about. Each row is paraphrased from the statute named in the right column.

QuestionUtah ruleStatute
Who is presumed to possess?The holder of legal title78B-2-208
How long must adverse use last?At least seven years78B-2-208, 78B-2-214
Are property taxes required?Yes, all levied and assessed taxes must be paid78B-2-214
Does a deed or judgment help?Yes, with seven years of continuous occupation78B-2-210
No paperwork at all?Only the land actually occupied counts78B-2-212
Tax title holder for four years?Presumed owner, unless the title holder was in possession or taxes went unpaid78B-2-209

What is the tax title presumption in Utah?

A person holding a tax title for four years before the lawsuit can be presumed the owner by adverse possession, but the presumption can be rebutted. Utah Code 78B-2-209 says the legal title owner can defeat it by showing they or a predecessor actually occupied or possessed the property under the title, or that the tax title holder failed to pay all taxes assessed during the four years.

This ties squatter law to property tax law. An owner who keeps paying the county bill and keeps visiting the property is hard to displace.

How can an owner remove a trespasser quickly in Utah?

Since May 7, 2025, an owner or authorized agent can ask law enforcement to remove a trespasser immediately by filing a verified complaint, without a lawsuit first. This limited remedy is in Utah Code 78B-6-817.

The owner must attest to all of the following.

  • The trespasser entered unlawfully and remains on the property.
  • The property was not open to the public when the person entered.
  • The owner told the trespasser to leave.
  • The trespasser is not a current or former tenant under a written rental agreement the owner authorized.
  • The trespasser is not an immediate family member.
  • No litigation about the property is pending between the owner and the trespasser.

The complaint is made under penalty of perjury and comes with proof of ownership and identification, or papers showing an agent's authority.

What happens after the complaint is filed?

If the owner appears entitled to relief, law enforcement serves a notice to immediately vacate, either by hand delivery or by posting it, and puts the owner in possession. Officers try to verify the trespasser's identity, and may arrest for trespass, outstanding warrants or another legal cause.

After service, the owner may ask officers to keep the peace while locks are changed and the trespasser's belongings are moved to or near the property line. Neither law enforcement nor the owner is liable for loss or damage to that property unless the removal was wrongful.

What is the risk of using the Utah removal process wrongly?

A person who is wrongfully removed can sue and be restored to possession. They may recover actual costs and damages, statutory damages equal to three times the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees, and the court must expedite the case.

The complaint form itself warns that false statements or wrongful use can make the owner liable. That is why the process excludes anyone with a written lease, current or former, and anyone in litigation with the owner. If the occupant claims a lease, or was a tenant, the usual route is the unlawful detainer process in 78B-6-802, which sets the notice periods for tenants who stay past a term, fail to pay rent or breach the lease.

Is squatting also a crime in Utah?

Entering or remaining unlawfully can be criminal trespass. Under Utah Code 76-6-206, a person commits it by remaining unlawfully with intent to cause annoyance, injury or damage, or by remaining on property after notice against entering given by personal communication, fencing or posted signs.

The offense is a class B misdemeanor, and a class A misdemeanor if committed in a dwelling. The owner may also recover statutory damages of three times the resulting damage or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees up to $250 and court costs. Criminal charges are separate from the civil right to recover possession.

How do vacant and inherited houses become squatter targets?

Vacant houses carry the most risk because no one is there to object. Utah law protects the owner who stays involved, which means a few habits go a long way.

  • Pay the property tax bill on time, since adverse possession requires the claimant to have paid.
  • Visit the property and keep notice against entering posted.
  • Tell trespassers in writing to leave and keep a record.
  • Keep proof of ownership ready, such as a recorded deed or letters from probate.

For an inherited house in a probate that has not been opened, ownership paperwork is often the missing piece. A family may need a personal representative before anyone can sign the complaint as owner.

When does selling make more sense than fighting for the house?

Selling can be the practical choice when an owner lives out of state, cannot supervise the property, or does not want to carry insurance and tax on a house that has become a liability. A cash buyer can purchase a house with an occupant problem as is, though the owner should clear possession issues through the legal routes above where possible.

If the house is vacant and the owner simply wants out, the sale does not require repairs or staging. If a trespasser is present, ask an attorney which route fits the facts before listing.

More questions about Utah Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in Utah?

At least seven years of continuous occupation under a claim of right, with all property taxes paid by the claimant and predecessors, under Utah Code 78B-2-208 and 78B-2-214.

Do squatters have rights in Utah?

Not automatically. Utah presumes the title holder is in possession. A squatter would have to prove seven years of continuous adverse possession and tax payment, and an owner may also use the 2025 trespasser removal process.

Can I have a squatter removed without going to court in Utah?

Often yes. Utah Code 78B-6-817 lets an owner file a verified complaint with law enforcement, which can serve a notice to vacate and put the owner in possession, if the six listed conditions are met.

What if the person in my house says they are a tenant?

The removal process excludes current or former tenants under a written rental agreement the owner authorized. A tenancy dispute goes through the unlawful detainer process under Utah Code 78B-6-802 instead.

What happens if I wrongly remove someone in Utah?

The person can sue for restoration of possession, actual damages, statutory damages of three times fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees under Utah Code 78B-6-817(5).

Utah statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord must return the deposit balance and prepaid rent, with a written itemization of any deductions, no later than 30 days after the renter vacates and returns possession. (Utah Code 57-17-3(2); source)
  • If the owner fails to comply, tenant may serve a statutory notice; owner then has five business days to comply or owe the full deposit, prepaid rent and a $100 penalty, and possibly court costs and attorney fees if bad faith. (Utah Code 57-17-3(3),(5); source)
  • Owner must give at least 24 hours prior notice of entry into the rental unit, unless the rental agreement provides otherwise. (Utah Code 57-22-4(2); source)
  • Owner may not rent premises unless safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and must maintain common areas, electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water, and any air conditioning in operable condition. (Utah Code 57-22-4(1); source)
  • Late fee may not exceed the greater of 10% of rent or $75; a new charge not in the rental agreement is allowed only on a month-to-month tenancy with 15-day notice. (Utah Code 57-22-4(5); source)
  • A tenant on a month-to-month (indefinite, periodic rent) tenancy must be served notice to quit at least 15 calendar days before the end of the month or period. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(b)(i); source)

What the official sources say

  • Lease violation: unlawful assignment/sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance or criminal act requires a three calendar days' notice to quit; other covenant violations require a written notice to perform or surrender, uncomplied for three calendar days. (Utah Code 78B-6-802(1)(d)-(h); source)

Which eviction notice does a Utah landlord use?

The notice depends on the problem: three days for unpaid rent or most lease violations, five days for a tenant with no lease, and at least 15 days to end a month-to-month rental.

Utah Courts publishes a separate form for each situation, and landlords are expected to match the form to the reason.

SituationCourt formNotice period
Unpaid rent1001EV3 days
Lease violation the tenant can fix1005EV3 days
Lease violation the tenant cannot fix1035EV3 days
Subletting without permission1020EV3 days
Nuisance (fixable or not)1015.5EV or 1015EV3 days
Criminal act on the property1040EV3 days
Illegal business1030EV3 days
Property damage or waste1025EV3 days
Lease ending, not renewed1045EVAt least 15 days before rent is due
Tenant at will, no lease1050EV5 days

These come from the court's landlord eviction guide. A landlord names every lease signer, tenant, subtenant and other occupant who needs to be removed, and can use John or Jane Doe for unknown occupants.

How are the notice days counted?

The day of service is day zero, and the count starts the next day.

Business days skip weekends and court holidays, while calendar days count everything. The difference matters most for unpaid rent, where the tenant has three business days to pay or move, and for rule violations, where the tenant has three calendar days. Utah Courts tells tenants to check that the notice was delivered properly and that the deadline was counted correctly, so both sides have a reason to get the arithmetic right.

For a month-to-month tenant, the 15 day notice must be served at least 15 days before the rental period ends. Served late, it does not end the tenancy until the next period closes.

How does a landlord deliver the notice?

Utah Code 78B-6-805 allows four ways to serve a notice, and a landlord has to use one of them.

  • Hand it to the tenant directly.
  • Mail it certified or registered, with a signature required, to the tenant's home.
  • If the tenant is away, leave it with another responsible adult at the home and mail a copy there too.
  • If no one is home, post it on the front door or another visible spot on the property.

Utah Courts also says that only a court order permits a legal eviction. Changing the locks, shutting off utilities, taking belongings or blocking the tenant from the home is prohibited.

What happens after the notice runs out?

If the tenant has not fixed the problem or left, the landlord files a complaint and summons, and the tenant has three business days after service to file an Answer.

The landlord cannot hand over the papers personally. Service goes through an adult 18 or older who is not part of the case, a sheriff or constable, or a process server, and must be completed within 120 days of filing. The notice and the lease are attached to the complaint as exhibits.

From there the case splits:

  • Tenant does not answer: the landlord can ask for a default judgment after checking military status. A servicemember may get a delay of up to 90 days.
  • Tenant answers, even late: no default is possible, and the landlord requests an occupancy hearing, which the court schedules within 10 days of the request.
  • Issues remain after the hearing: a trial is set within 60 days.

At the occupancy hearing, the judge decides who stays while the case continues and may sign an Order of Restitution against the tenant.

How fast does a tenant have to leave after the order?

The Order of Restitution usually gives the tenant three calendar days after service to move out, and a sheriff or constable can remove the tenant after that.

Only a sheriff or deputy, police officer, constable, state investigator or licensed private investigator can serve the order, and a landlord cannot serve it personally. Only after proper service and the tenant's departure, or a sheriff's removal, can the landlord retake the property under Utah Code 78B-6-812.

StageWindow
Answer to the complaint3 business days after service
Occupancy hearingWithin 10 days of the request
Trial if neededWithin 60 days
Move out after the orderUsually 3 calendar days
Access to essential items5 business days
Other belongings treated as abandoned15 calendar days

Essential items include clothing, ID, financial and immigration papers, and medical items, and no storage fee can be charged for them. A tenant who cannot leave in time can ask the court to set aside the judgment or to delay enforcement, and delay requires a bond.

What can a landlord recover in money?

A landlord can ask for unpaid rent, repair costs and daily rental value after the notice expired, and several of those amounts can be tripled.

Utah Courts lists the recoverable items as unpaid rent, property damage, the daily rental value after the notice expired (up to three times), forcible entry costs, repairs and nuisance removal costs (each up to three times). The landlord has to prove the amounts and try to re-rent the home promptly. The tenant's side of the court site gives a sample: rent of $900 a month is $30 a day, so 30 holdover days could be $2,700 when trebled.

A tenant has seven days to object to the affidavit of damages. A money judgment is separate from the eviction, so moving out does not erase it.

Which special rules can change the process?

Several situations call for extra checks before a landlord starts, and any of them can add time.

  • Government rent help, such as Section 8 or a voucher.
  • A tenant who owns a mobile home but rents the land, covered by the Utah Mobile Home Park Residency Act.
  • A property loan owned by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, or a home foreclosed with a federally backed loan.
  • A business owner, since a business without a DBA needs a representative in court.

Tenants can also post a possession bond. In an unpaid rent case, a tenant who pays everything owed within three calendar days can stay and the case ends.

How does an eviction affect selling a Utah house?

A Utah owner with a tenant in place has to finish the court process or reach a voluntary move-out before the house can be handed over empty.

The stages above add up, and a contested case that goes to trial takes longer. The case also leaves a mark, since Utah Courts tells tenants that an eviction case stays on the record permanently, which gives some tenants a reason to negotiate a move-out instead.

Owners in this spot often choose between waiting out the court calendar, negotiating a move-out date, or selling the house with the tenant in it. We buy Utah houses in any of those conditions, and we can talk through the sequence with you before you pay for a notice or a filing.

More questions about Utah Eviction Notice Rules

How many days notice does a Utah landlord give for unpaid rent?

Three business days. The tenant can pay what is owed or move out in that time, and day zero is the day the notice is delivered.

How long does a Utah landlord have to give a month-to-month tenant?

At least 15 days, served before the end of the rental period. If it is served too late, the tenant can stay until the next period ends.

How long does a tenant have to respond to a Utah eviction complaint?

Three business days after being served with the summons and complaint. Missing that deadline can mean losing the case automatically.

Can a Utah landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Only a court order allows a legal eviction, and changing locks, cutting utilities or removing belongings is prohibited.

How long does a tenant have to leave after an Order of Restitution?

Usually three calendar days after service of the order, though it can be less. A sheriff or constable can remove the tenant after that.
